title: Christmas in Tbilisi: Markets & New Year Travel Guide
excerpt: Plan Christmas and New Year in Tbilisi with clear holiday dates, market checks, neighbourhood advice and a flexible three-day festive itinerary.
metaTitle: Christmas in Tbilisi: Markets & New Year Travel Guide
metaDescription: Plan Christmas in Tbilisi with Georgian holiday dates, market updates, hotel-area advice and a three-day itinerary for a relaxed Christmas and New Year trip.

children.text: Christmas in Tbilisi is easier to plan once you separate three things: the city's festive markets, New Year's Eve on 31 December and Georgian Orthodox Christmas on 7 January. They are related, but they do not share one opening date or one programme. This guide helps you choose your travel window, find the right area to stay and build a manageable holiday in Georgia's capital.

Planning note, checked 27 October 2026: we have not verified an official municipal programme for the 2026/27 season. Market locations, opening dates, concerts and special transport hours below must be confirmed for your travel dates. Historical examples are labelled as such.
When is Christmas in Tbilisi?

Georgian Orthodox Christmas falls on 7 January, so the upcoming celebration is 7 January 2027. New Year's Eve remains 31 December 2026. If your holiday is built around 25 December, you can still plan a winter city break, but do not expect that date to be the main Georgian Christmas celebration.
Georgia's National Tourism Administration describes
Alilo

, the Christmas tradition of singing and collecting gifts for people in need, as a 7 January celebration. It is a cultural and religious occasion, rather than another name for the commercial Christmas market.

A second tradition is Old New Year, celebrated on 14 January. That does not establish how long any particular market, restaurant programme or skating rink will operate. Book your trip around the experience you want, then verify the event that matters to you.
Which travel window should you choose?
Late December before New Year's Eve: a candidate for a lights-and-markets city break, once the current programme is confirmed.
31 December into early January: choose this if the countdown and a planned celebration are your priority.
Around 6–7 January: choose this if Georgian Christmas and Alilo matter most.
Later in January: suitable for a winter visit, but do not assume festive stalls will still be trading.

For a short trip, choose one priority. Trying to include New Year's Eve and Georgian Christmas requires a longer stay than a three-night weekend. Decide whether the extra nights add experiences you want before stretching the budget.
Tbilisi Christmas market 2026/27: what is confirmed?
The city's main festive market is often described as the New Year Village. For the previous 2025/26 season,
Tbilisi City Hall's published programme
placed it on First Republic Square from 12 December to 7 January, with food and craft stalls and performances.

Those are historical dates, not a confirmed schedule for December 2026. As of this guide's check date, we have not verified a new official announcement establishing the 2026/27 opening, location or daily hours.

Before reserving a hotel specifically for a market, check the current City Hall announcement. For a privately organised fair, use the organiser's own dated event page or booking confirmation. A hotel craft fair on one Sunday is a different event from a municipal village running over several weeks.

When checking an event listing, look for all four details: the year, exact venue, operating dates and admission arrangements. If a page simply says “December to January,” that is not enough to plan an arrival night around.
How to plan an evening of lights and markets

Choose one central area and one meal stop rather than attempting to cross the whole city after dark. Rustaveli Avenue, Freedom Square and the Old Town provide useful geographic reference points, but the year's actual decorations and event locations should determine your evening route.

For a market visit, arrive with enough flexibility to leave if it is crowded, wet or too cold for your group. Buy food when you are ready to eat, then leave time to browse craft stalls without turning the evening into a shopping checklist.

Ask about ingredients before ordering unfamiliar sweets or hot drinks. Keep a small amount of local currency for purchases, while checking whether each stall accepts cards. Do not assume every seasonal seller has the same payment options or refund policy.

If you are travelling with children, plan a warm indoor break before anyone gets tired. One good hour outdoors followed by dinner can be more enjoyable than waiting through a full stage programme. Keep the return journey as simple as the outing.
New Year in Tbilisi: choose your evening before booking

The most useful decision is whether you want a restaurant celebration, a hotel evening or a short outing followed by a quiet night. There is no single version of New Year's Eve that suits every traveller.
A restaurant or hotel celebration

Request the actual 31 December offer rather than relying on the venue's ordinary menu. Ask whether the price includes drinks, entertainment, service charges and a table for the whole evening. Confirm children's arrangements, dietary requests and the cancellation deadline before paying.

For an alcohol-free or halal-friendly evening, explain your requirements directly. A vegetable dish on the regular menu does not establish the ingredients of a festive set menu, and a family-friendly venue may still run a loud late-night programme.
A public celebration
Use a current official announcement to confirm any concert, meeting point and access restrictions. Do not assume that a previous year's stage, programme or fireworks arrangement will be repeated.

Choose an exit route before joining a crowd, and avoid standing close to people setting off fireworks. With younger children or anyone sensitive to noise, an earlier walk or a quiet indoor setting may be more comfortable than a midnight gathering.
A quieter evening

You can enjoy the season without a large party. Arrange dinner near your accommodation, take a short walk if conditions suit and return at your own pace. When booking a room, ask about street noise, adjoining event spaces and any compulsory gala dinner.
Where to stay for a festive Tbilisi trip
Choose accommodation by walking route, access and comfort, not simply by the word “central.” A property can be close on a map yet involve steep lanes, stairs or an awkward approach with luggage.

The Freedom Square and lower Rustaveli area is a useful starting point for comparing central hotels. Look at the actual distance to your chosen restaurant and any confirmed event venue. A room facing a busy street may suit someone who wants atmosphere but disappoint someone seeking an early night.

Sololaki and the Old Town offer a different setting, with smaller streets and characterful buildings. Ask about heating, lift access and the number of steps to the room. For a family using a pushchair, those practical details deserve as much attention as the photographs.
Our
guide to where to stay in Georgia

explains the main Tbilisi neighbourhood choices. For the festive period, add three questions: can you walk back comfortably, is breakfast available on your dates, and are any holiday meals compulsory?
Georgian Christmas, Alilo and seasonal food

If your visit includes 7 January, leave space in the day for Alilo rather than attaching it to a tightly timed transfer. Confirm the procession's current route and start time near your visit; this guide does not treat the January 2026 timetable as a January 2027 announcement.

If visiting a working church, follow posted guidance and the congregation's lead. Keep your phone quiet, ask before photographing people at close range and avoid obstructing worshippers. You can appreciate the occasion without attending every part of a service.
Look out for a chichilaki, the Georgian festive tree made from curled wood shavings. The tourism administration's explanation of
Old New Year traditions
describes its hazelnut-wood construction and decoration with fruit and sweets. It is a more specifically Georgian seasonal symbol than another imported ornament.

Gozinaki, a sweet commonly made with walnuts and honey, is another holiday-table favourite. Treat it as food to enjoy and share, while checking ingredients if anyone has a nut allergy. For gifts, choose products with clear labels and packaging suitable for your journey.
A flexible three-day festive itinerary
This is a planning framework, not an advertised event programme. Move the market evening to a confirmed operating date and replace it with an indoor activity if the weather is poor.
Day 1: settle in and keep the evening short

Check in, learn the route back to your hotel and take a manageable walk near your accommodation. If a market is operating, use the first evening for a brief look rather than a long queue or a late dinner. A late-arriving flight is a good reason to save the main outing for tomorrow.
Day 2: see the city, then choose one festive activity
Use daylight for sightseeing and leave a break before going out again. TripMate's
private half-day Tbilisi city tour
is a bookable option for a guided introduction. Ask about holiday availability and the route on your date; the city tour is not a Christmas-event ticket.

In the evening, choose either a confirmed market visit or a reserved celebration. Avoid combining a long guided day, a separate excursion and a midnight programme simply because all three fit on a calendar.
Day 3: slow down before departure
Choose a relaxed breakfast and one activity that fits your flight time. A pre-booked bath session can be an option if the venue is open; our
Tbilisi sulfur baths guide
explains how to compare rooms and bookings.

If you are staying through 7 January, adjust the itinerary around your Christmas plans. Leave room for changed opening hours and city access rather than promising yourself a fixed sequence of museums and restaurants.
Weather, clothing and getting around

Plan for cold outdoor evenings and check the forecast close to departure. Do not book Christmas in Tbilisi on the assumption that the streets will be snowy. A city holiday and a snow-focused mountain holiday need different expectations.

Bring layers, a warm outer coat and footwear with grip. For children, spare socks and gloves can make it easier to recover from a wet outing. Keep a practical indoor alternative for each day rather than relying on every activity taking place outside.

Check current public-transport notices for the festive nights. Special late services or free travel from a previous year should not be assumed for 2026/27. Save your accommodation address offline and decide where a driver could collect you if streets near an event are closed.
For arrival arrangements, use our
Tbilisi airport transport guide
. A pre-arranged pickup can be useful after a late flight, but confirm the meeting point and any delay policy.
What to budget and confirm before paying

Build the budget in separate parts: accommodation, airport transport, ordinary meals, a special dinner if wanted, tours and shopping. Ask for prices in a clearly stated currency and check whether an advertised amount is per person, per room or per vehicle.

For example, a dinner quotation of 180 GEL per adult would mean 360 GEL for two adults before any excluded drinks or service charges. This is a calculation example, not a verified restaurant price or a forecast of New Year's Eve costs.
Confirm these details before making a non-refundable booking:
The event or meal is operating on your exact date.
Your room, table or tour is confirmed for the correct number of adults and children.
Dietary needs, mobility needs and child-seat requests have been acknowledged.
The total price, inclusions and cancellation terms are clear.
You have a workable return journey.
The best festive itinerary leaves room for a change of plan. Start with the celebration you actually want, book the few things that need certainty, and keep the remaining time flexible.

faq.question: When is Christmas celebrated in Tbilisi?
faq.answer: Georgian Orthodox Christmas is on 7 January, so the upcoming celebration is 7 January 2027. New Year's Eve is on 31 December 2026. A visit on 25 December is a different travel window from the main Georgian Christmas celebration.

faq.question: When does the Tbilisi Christmas market open in 2026?
faq.answer: As of our check on 27 October 2026, we have not verified an official municipal opening date for the 2026/27 season. The previous season's programme ran from 12 December to 7 January on First Republic Square. Check the new City Hall announcement before booking around a market date.

faq.question: Does it snow in Tbilisi at Christmas?
faq.answer: Snow is possible, but it is not something to build a fixed city itinerary around. Check the forecast before travelling, pack for cold evenings and keep indoor alternatives. A trip primarily intended for snow needs separate mountain planning.

faq.question: Is Tbilisi at Christmas suitable for families?
faq.answer: It can suit families who keep outings manageable, choose accommodation with good access and plan warm indoor breaks. Confirm children's arrangements for dinners and events. Midnight crowds and fireworks may be uncomfortable for younger children or anyone sensitive to noise.

faq.question: How many days do you need for a festive Tbilisi visit?
faq.answer: Three full days provide a useful framework for city sightseeing, one confirmed festive outing and a slower activity. To experience both New Year's Eve and Georgian Christmas on 7 January, allow a longer stay spanning those dates.

cta.title: Plan your festive Tbilisi trip
cta.description: Build a Georgia itinerary around your travel dates, family needs and the celebrations you want to experience. Keep confirmed bookings together and leave room for winter flexibility.
